title: Unrestricted madvise in VMM thread allows guest-triggered host memory manipulation
description: The VMM thread's seccomp filter allows the madvise() syscall with no argument restrictions whatsoever, while the API and vCPU threads correctly restrict it to MADV_DONTNEED only. This means a compromised VMM thread (via a bug in device emulation triggered by guest I/O) can call madvise() with any advice value, including MADV_HUGEPAGE, MADV_DONTFORK, MADV_REMOVE (which can punch holes in files backing tmpfs/shmem), or MADV_FREE (which can discard dirty pages and cause data loss on the host). The same unrestricted madvise exists on the aarch64 filter. This is particularly dangerous because the VMM thread processes all device I/O from the guest.
impact: A guest VM exploiting a device emulation bug can use arbitrary madvise operations on host memory. MADV_REMOVE can cause data destruction on tmpfs/shmem-backed memory regions. MADV_DONTFORK can cause host child processes to access zeroed memory instead of expected data. MADV_HWPOISON can trigger hardware error injection on the host.
attack_path: 1. Guest crafts malicious VirtIO device I/O that triggers a bug in VMM device emulation code (e.g., balloon, pmem, or net). 2. Attacker gains code execution or controlled madvise call in the VMM thread context. 3. Attacker calls madvise() with MADV_REMOVE on a file-backed mapping to punch holes in the underlying file, or MADV_HWPOISON to inject memory errors, which are not filtered by seccomp.
evidence: resources/seccomp/x86_64-unknown-linux-musl.json:219-221 - VMM filter has madvise with no args restrictions. Compare with resources/seccomp/x86_64-unknown-linux-musl.json:894-904 (API thread) and :1146-1156 (vCPU thread) which both restrict to MADV_DONTNEED only.
remediation: Add argument filtering to the VMM thread's madvise entry to only allow the specific advice values needed: MADV_DONTNEED (4), MADV_WIPEONFORK (18), and MADV_NORMAL (0). Block dangerous values like MADV_REMOVE (9), MADV_HWPOISON (100), and MADV_FREE (8).

title: TOCTOU race in chroot_dir creation allows symlink-based redirection
description: The jailer's main_exec() in main.rs first calls Env::new() which canonicalizes chroot_base at line 159 of env.rs and builds a chroot_dir path, then separately calls fs::create_dir_all(env.chroot_dir()) at line 354 of main.rs. Between the canonicalization and the directory creation, the intermediate path components (chroot_base/<exec_file_name>/<id>/) are not created atomically. A local attacker with write access to the parent of the chroot base directory could race to replace one of these intermediate directories with a symlink after canonicalization but before create_dir_all, redirecting the chroot to an attacker-controlled location. The canonicalize only resolves symlinks at the time it is called. If an attacker replaces a path component between canonicalize and create_dir_all, create_dir_all will follow the new symlink.
impact: A local attacker who can write to the chroot-base-dir parent can redirect the chroot jail to an arbitrary filesystem location, potentially causing Firecracker to pivot_root into an attacker-controlled directory. This would negate all jailer isolation.
attack_path: 1. Attacker observes jailer being launched with --chroot-base-dir /srv/jailer. 2. Between Env::new() canonicalizing /srv/jailer (env.rs:159) and fs::create_dir_all() creating the nested hierarchy (main.rs:354), attacker replaces /srv/jailer/<exec_name> with a symlink to /tmp/evil-root. 3. create_dir_all follows the symlink and creates the jail under /tmp/evil-root/<id>/root. 4. Firecracker's chroot and pivot_root operate on the attacker-controlled directory.
evidence: src/jailer/src/env.rs:159-168 (canonicalize then build path) and src/jailer/src/main.rs:354 (create_dir_all with time gap). The copy_exec_to_chroot at env.rs:489-495 uses O_NOFOLLOW for the destination file, but the directory structure itself is not protected.
remediation: Use O_NOFOLLOW when creating each component of the chroot directory hierarchy. Open the chroot base directory with O_PATH|O_NOFOLLOW and create subdirectories relative to the file descriptor using mkdirat(). Alternatively, create the full path atomically and verify with fstat that no component is a symlink.

title: Custom seccomp filter (--seccomp-filter) allows arbitrary filter weakening with no validation
description: The --seccomp-filter flag accepts a path to a user-provided binary BPF filter file. In seccomp.rs, get_custom_filters() at line 74 deserializes the user-provided binary and only validates that it contains the correct thread category keys (vmm, api, vcpu). It performs no validation that the filters actually restrict any syscalls. A user (or an attacker who can write to the filter file) can provide a filter that allows all syscalls, effectively making Firecracker run with no seccomp protection at all. Unlike --no-seccomp which is an explicit opt-out, --seccomp-filter provides a false sense of security since seccomp appears to be 'enabled' while providing no actual protection. Additionally, the apply_filter() function in seccomp.rs:94-97 silently skips installation when the BPF program is empty (len == 0), so a custom filter with empty programs results in no seccomp at all.
impact: An attacker who can modify the seccomp filter file on disk, or an operator who provides a permissive filter, can completely disable seccomp sandboxing while the system reports that custom seccomp filtering is active. This removes a critical defense-in-depth layer.
attack_path: 1. Attacker gains write access to the seccomp filter file path provided via --seccomp-filter. 2. Attacker replaces the file with a binary containing empty BPF programs for vmm/api/vcpu categories. 3. Firecracker loads the filters successfully (passes filter_thread_categories check). 4. apply_filter() at seccomp.rs:96-97 sees empty programs and returns Ok(()) without installing any filter. 5. All threads run without any seccomp restrictions.
evidence: src/vmm/src/seccomp.rs:94-98 (apply_filter skips empty filters), src/firecracker/src/seccomp.rs:74-77 (no validation of filter content), src/firecracker/src/seccomp.rs:80-105 (filter_thread_categories only checks key names).
remediation: Add validation that custom filters are non-empty and contain at least one actual BPF instruction per thread category. Consider logging a warning when custom filters are significantly simpler than the default filters. Consider requiring a minimum filter that blocks the most dangerous syscalls (e.g., execve, clone with CLONE_NEWUSER).

title: Cgroup value injection allows writing to arbitrary cgroup knobs via crafted values
description: The jailer's cgroup value parsing at env.rs:229-245 splits on '=' and validates that the file component (left of '=') does not contain path traversal characters. However, the value component (right of '=') undergoes no validation at all. The value is written directly to cgroup files via writeln_special() at cgroup.rs:363 and :472. For cgroupsv2, the cgroup subtree_control file is writable (cgroup.rs:401) and accepts '+controller' format. While the file name is validated, the value written to legitimate cgroup files is unchecked. A malicious value containing newlines could potentially inject multiple lines into cgroup control files. More critically, for cgroupsv1, if an attacker can influence the cgroup arguments, they can set dangerous values like memory.limit_in_bytes=9999999999999999 (effectively unlimited) or cpuset.cpus=0-99999 to attempt resource escape.
impact: An attacker who controls jailer arguments (e.g., via a management API) can set arbitrary cgroup values that may weaken resource isolation. Setting overly permissive cgroup values can allow the jailed process to consume more resources than intended, potentially affecting other VMs on the same host.
attack_path: 1. Attacker controls the --cgroup arguments passed to the jailer (e.g., through an orchestration layer). 2. Attacker passes --cgroup memory.limit_in_bytes=max or --cgroup cpu.cfs_quota_us=-1 (which means unlimited in cgroupsv1). 3. The jailer writes these values without validation. 4. The jailed Firecracker process runs with effectively unlimited resources.
evidence: src/jailer/src/env.rs:229-242 (value not validated, only file name checked), src/jailer/src/cgroup.rs:349-351 (CgroupV1::add_property stores value without validation), src/jailer/src/cgroup.rs:363 (writeln_special writes raw value), src/jailer/src/main.rs:243 (writeln_special called with fmt format, allowing arbitrary content).
remediation: Add validation for cgroup values: reject values containing newlines, null bytes, or path separators. Consider maintaining an allowlist of safe cgroup properties and their valid value ranges. At minimum, validate that values are single-line and contain only printable ASCII characters.

title: Network namespace path (--netns) not validated against symlink or TOCTOU attacks
description: The join_netns() function at env.rs:520-529 opens the provided --netns path using File::open() without O_NOFOLLOW or any validation that the path points to an actual network namespace file (under /var/run/netns/ or /proc/*/ns/net). The open happens before chroot, so it has access to the full host filesystem. An attacker who can influence the --netns argument or race the filesystem can use a symlink to cause the jailer to join an arbitrary namespace. File::open follows symlinks by default. There is also a TOCTOU race: the namespace file could be replaced between the open and the setns call, though the fd semantics mitigate this somewhat.
impact: An attacker who can control the --netns argument or create a symlink at the target path can cause the jailer to join an unexpected network namespace, potentially providing the jailed VM with network access it should not have, or placing it in a namespace where it can sniff traffic from other VMs.
attack_path: 1. Attacker creates a symlink at the expected netns path pointing to /proc/1/ns/net (the host's init network namespace). 2. Jailer opens the symlink-resolved path and calls setns() to join the host network namespace. 3. The jailed Firecracker process has full host network access. Alternatively: attacker points to another VM's netns, enabling cross-VM network sniffing.
evidence: src/jailer/src/env.rs:520-529 (File::open without O_NOFOLLOW, no path validation), src/jailer/src/env.rs:646-648 (join_netns called before chroot).
remediation: Open the netns path with O_NOFOLLOW|O_PATH to prevent symlink following. Validate that the path is under an expected directory (/var/run/netns/ or /proc/*/ns/net). Use fstat after open to verify the file type is correct (S_IFREG for namespace files).

title: Unrestricted open() syscall in all thread filters enables arbitrary file access from jail
description: The seccomp filters for all three thread categories (vmm, api, vcpu) allow the open() syscall with no argument restrictions. This means any thread in the Firecracker process can open any file accessible within the chroot jail (or on the host if running without the jailer). Combined with the also-unrestricted read() and write() syscalls, this gives full file I/O capability to all threads. While the chroot jail limits the visible filesystem, if an attacker achieves code execution within the Firecracker process (e.g., via a guest-triggered device emulation bug), they can access all files within the jail, including the firecracker binary itself, device backing files, and the API socket.
impact: A guest VM that exploits a device emulation vulnerability gains unrestricted file access within the chroot jail. This includes reading the firecracker binary (for further exploit development), accessing other VMs' block device files if they share the jail (misconfiguration), and accessing the API socket to reconfigure the VM.
attack_path: 1. Guest exploits a bug in VirtIO device emulation to gain code execution in the VMM thread. 2. Attacker uses the unrestricted open/read/write syscalls to access the API socket at /run/firecracker.socket. 3. Attacker sends API commands to reconfigure the VM or load a malicious snapshot. 4. Alternatively, attacker reads block device files of other VMs if co-located in the same chroot (deployment error).
evidence: resources/seccomp/x86_64-unknown-linux-musl.json:23-24 (vmm open unrestricted), :747-748 (api open unrestricted), :1039-1040 (vcpu open unrestricted). All three lack any argument-based filtering (e.g., O_RDONLY restriction).
remediation: Consider restricting the open() syscall to O_RDONLY where possible, especially for the vCPU thread which should not need write access to files. Use openat2() with RESOLVE_NO_SYMLINKS where available. For the API thread, restrict open to specific flags needed for socket operations.

title: Chroot directory creation race allows local user to influence jail contents
description: The jailer creates the chroot directory hierarchy at main.rs:354 using fs::create_dir_all(), then copies the exec file and sets up the jail environment inside it. Between directory creation and the pivot_root at chroot.rs, there is a window where a local user with write access to intermediate path components could inject files or symlinks into the jail directory. Specifically, the sequence is: 1) create_dir_all(chroot_dir) [main.rs:354], 2) copy_exec_to_chroot [env.rs:642], 3) setup cgroups [env.rs:654], 4) chroot [env.rs:673]. Between steps 1 and 4, the chroot directory is on the host filesystem with its parent directories potentially world-readable (depending on chroot-base-dir permissions). While the folder permissions are set to 0o700, this is done after chroot inside setup_jailed_folder, not during initial creation.
impact: A local attacker could place files in the jail directory between its creation and the pivot_root, potentially injecting a malicious binary that replaces the exec file or adding device nodes that bypass the intended jail restrictions.
attack_path: 1. Attacker monitors for new directory creation under /srv/jailer/. 2. After create_dir_all creates the directory hierarchy but before pivot_root, attacker places a malicious file in the new directory. 3. If the attacker can race copy_exec_to_chroot (which uses create, not create_new for all code paths), they could influence the jail contents.
evidence: src/jailer/src/main.rs:354 (create_dir_all without restricted permissions), src/jailer/src/env.rs:642-673 (sequence with time gaps between operations), src/jailer/src/env.rs:456-458 (FOLDER_PERMISSIONS 0o700 set after chroot, not during initial creation at line 354).
remediation: Create the chroot directory with restricted permissions (0o700) from the start by using mkdir with explicit mode instead of create_dir_all. Set umask to 0o077 before creating any directories. Consider using mkdirat with O_NOFOLLOW on a validated parent fd to prevent symlink attacks at each level.
